steps.label: The acceptor
steps.margin_note: Full name with the carbon count. Watch the spelling of bisphosphate.
lines: The primary acceptor of CO2 in C3 plants is
steps.why: A 5-carbon acceptor taking one carbon gives a 6-carbon compound, which is why the product splits into two 3-carbon molecules.
common_mistakes: Naming PEP. PEP is the C4 acceptor, not the C3 one.
Writing 'biphosphate'. It is BISphosphate — two separate phosphate groups.
steps.memory_tip: RuBP has five carbons and catches the sixth.

steps.label: The first stable compound
steps.margin_note: Name it, give the carbon count, and connect it to the name C3.

lines.text: RuBP (5C) catches CO2; PGA (3C) is what forms

lines: The first stable compound is PGA —
It is a 3-carbon compound, which is why the
pathway is called the C3 cycle.
steps.why: The pathway is named after the first stable product, so the carbon count here explains the name of the whole cycle.
common_mistakes: Naming OAA. OAA is the first C4 product.
Leaving out the carbon count. Three carbons is why it is called C3.
steps.memory_tip: Three carbons in the first product names the whole cycle.
